image.alt: A Philodendron Xanadu in a white pot, its deeply lobed glossy green leaves spreading into a low mound

light.label: Bright indirect light, or morning sun outdoors
light.note: Takes medium light indoors and morning sun outdoors

snap: A compact, self-heading Philodendron with deeply lobed, glossy leaves that spread into a low mound. It holds its shape without a pole, takes more light than most Philodendrons, and is toxic to cats and dogs if chewed.

deep_dive.title: Origin & Habit
deep_dive.body: Native to Brazil, and moved out of Philodendron into the genus Thaumatophyllum in 2018 — the trade still sells it under the old name. It is self-heading rather than climbing, settling into a mound around three feet across and about as tall.

deep_dive.title: Key Care Rule
deep_dive.body: Water when the top inch of soil has dried. Thick stems hold enough in reserve to forgive a missed week, but it sulks in soggy soil, so drainage matters more than frequency. Outdoors keep it out of harsh afternoon sun, which bleaches the leaves.

deep_dive.title: Special Feature
deep_dive.body: Most Philodendrons climb and want a moss pole. This one keeps its own shape, which is what makes it work as a floor plant indoors and as mass planting outdoors with no support at all. The deeply cut leaves read almost fern-like from across a room.

deep_dive.title: Indoors Or Out
deep_dive.body: Happy in a pot by a bright window and equally happy in the ground in a frost-free garden, where it takes morning sun and spreads into low, weed-smothering cover. Few houseplants do both this well.

deep_dive.title: Pet Safety
deep_dive.body: Toxic to cats and dogs if chewed or swallowed; the calcium oxalate crystals irritate the mouth and stomach. Its low, spreading habit puts the leaves right at pet height, so place it with that in mind.
